newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran steps up quake relief, digs for survivors.
newsitem.headline: Iran steps up quake relief, digs for survivors.

text.p: Villagers digging with spades and their bare hands on Monday pulled out a woman alive from the rubble of her home two days after an earthquake killed about 2,400 people in eastern Iran.

The group of 50 men searching for survivors in the ruins of their mountain hamlet called for silence after hearing faint cries from under her house flattened by Saturday's quake which measured 7.1 on the Richter scale.

Having located the voice, the men dug slowly and rescued the badly injured middle-aged woman named Maryam after a bulldozer supplied by the provincial relief agency removed some of the heavier debris.
But the quake did not spare the young in Ardakul near its epicentre. It also injured 6,000 and flattened 200 villages.
Sixty students aged between six and 12 at one school died.
Some pupils gathered beside all that remained of the school -- a 20 foot-high pile of mangled wooden and metal desks -- as a flock of about 200 goats gnawed at scattered books.
A mathematics book with the name of a girl named Zahra Yary lay in the rubble beside a pencil, ruler and a hairpin.
A nearby school's 73 students were out for lunch when the quake struck. But 30 pupils and two teachers died at home.
Survivors were still wandering in the ruins of their homes and burying their dead while waiting for international aid in response to a government appeal.
President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani visited stricken areas and pledged that the government would help rebuild the villages and construct quake-resistant buildings, Tehran radio said.
Army trucks delivered bags of rice and potatoes to Ardakul and water tankers also provided relief to dazed residents. Some 50 tents had been set up by the Iranian Red Crescent.
In the village of Hadjiabad, soldiers stocked rice bags, potatoes, biscuits and medical supplies in a hangar for distribution in the remote area near the Afghan border.
An elderly man covered in dust pushed a wheelbarrow with all he was able to salvage -- a blanket and a sewing machine.
Sargol Nadi, a civil servant who lost his six-year-old daughter, recalled the horror.
"Many people ran out of their homes when it hit. Those who remained inside died. The quake was slow. It got stronger and the walls collapsed," he said.
Some of those who were lucky enough to still own a home suffered more painful losses.
"I just don't know what to do," said Mohammad Reza Mehdiabadi, sitting in his home. He lost his 11-year-old daughter.
In Tehran, an Iranian Red Crescent spokesman said rescue workers would comb the quake-stricken areas one more time for survivors and bodies before winding up their operations.
The government said it would pay 500,000 rials ($167) to every person who lost a relative, Iran's news agency IRNA said.
United Nations and Iranian officials said the death toll from the quake which also left 50,000 homeless was unlikely to change dramatically as rescue work was nearly concluded.
U.N. officials in Tehran said rescue and relief efforts were going well but added that international assistance was needed to replenish the Red Crescent's stocks of food.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies appealed on Monday for $8.2 million to help Iran.
Quake-prone Iran, accustomed to dealing with natural disasters, has appealed through the United Nations for aid.
Iran's Gulf Arab neighbours Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates said they were flying in aid. So did Egypt.
France said it was sending a 30-strong rescue squad backed by sniffer dogs and a first French plane carrying 39 tonnes of emergency equipment and medicine had already landed in Iran.

The United States pledged $100,000 and United Nations agencies $350,000. Turkey said it would send two plane loads of emergency aid. Germany pledged 500,000 marks ($290,000) and Italy said it was giving supplies worth about $300,000.
Initial estimates put the extent of damage at up to 300 billion rials ($100 million), Tehran radio said on Monday.
Some 4,300 relief workers have set up 9,000 tents and Iran has asked for food, medicine, tents, water tanks and clothing.
